quickPanel.funFact: The name is short for “Network Mapper”, and it really does treat a network like a map.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: Nmap is a packet choreography engine. You give it a target set and a goal, and it decides which probes to send, in what order, and how to interpret the replies. “Scanning ports” is the visible output, but the hidden work is building a model of reachability and behavior from imperfect signals.

For TCP, Nmap leans on the fact that different responses imply different states. A SYN probe that receives a SYN/ACK suggests a listening service, while an RST suggests a reachable host with nothing listening on that port. If nothing comes back, Nmap has to decide whether it was dropped, filtered, rate limited, or lost on the path. That decision is why timing, retries, and host discovery choices matter so much.

Host discovery is its own phase. Nmap can use ICMP, TCP, UDP, or combinations to decide which hosts are “up”. Skipping discovery changes the meaning of later results, because you are now assuming the host exists and pushing straight to port probes. In practice, the boundary between discovery and scanning is fuzzy: a “closed” reply can also be a discovery signal.

Version detection and scripting are a second layer of probing. Once a port looks reachable, Nmap can talk just enough application protocol to guess what is running there. It uses a database of probes and match rules, so the output is essentially “this response pattern looks like X”. Scripts add yet another layer: they run targeted application level checks to extract metadata or test for known conditions. This is powerful, but it also increases assumptions and noise.

One mental model that helps: Nmap is not reading a static truth. It is sampling a live system under constraints. Every probe you send can change how the target behaves, because middleboxes and hosts respond differently under load, under throttling, or when they notice unusual traffic.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: The biggest trap is treating Nmap output as ground truth. It is evidence, and evidence has error bars. “Filtered” means Nmap did not get the definitive reply it expected, not that the port does not exist. “Closed” usually means the host was reachable enough to say no. “Open” means you got a reply that strongly suggests a listener, but even that can be spoofed by a firewall policy, a tarpitting service, or a proxy in front.

False negatives happen when the network drops probes, when a firewall rate limits, or when you scan from a path that is asymmetric. A classic example is scanning a host through a VPN or NAT where return traffic is shaped differently. The scan looks clean from one side and “filtered everywhere” from another, even though the host did not change.

False positives are rarer but real. Port forwarding can make many hosts appear to “share” open ports. Transparent proxies can make an HTTP service appear present on ports where the origin host never spoke HTTP. With version detection, custom banners can trick fingerprinting, and load balancers can expose one backend’s banner while routing you to another backend’s behavior.

Treat each line as a claim you should be able to defend. If you see an open port, ask: is the host definitely reachable, and is the port state stable across time. If you see a guessed service, ask: what did Nmap actually match on, and could a middlebox be answering. When you build that habit, Nmap becomes a reasoning tool instead of a magic oracle.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: Nmap’s capability space is best understood as a set of knobs that trade stealth, speed, and certainty. Scan type changes what packets are used and therefore what evidence you collect. Port selection changes coverage and time. Timing changes how hard you push the network and the target, which affects both detection risk and accuracy.

Flags and features cluster into categories. Discovery options decide whether you spend time proving a host is alive. Scan options decide how you ask about ports, and how you treat the privileges you have. Enrichment options decide whether you accept “open” as enough, or whether you attempt to identify services, versions, and scripts. Output options decide whether the scan is a one off glance or a reusable artifact.

The more enrichment you add, the more you move from transport level observation into application level interaction. That is where you can extract real value, but it is also where you can cause side effects. Even a simple banner grab can trigger logs, authentication banners, or rate limits. Script categories push further into “active testing”, which is why separating discovery from enrichment is a clean way to control risk.

Another dimension is vantage point. Nmap run from inside a network is a different instrument than Nmap run from outside. The difference is not just “more ports open internally”. It is that internal scanning interacts with different ACLs, different routing, and often different DNS and service discovery. The same host can legitimately look like two different machines depending on where you stand.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: Nmap is best used when you need a map, not a microscope. It answers “what appears reachable from here” and “what does it look like”, which is ideal for asset discovery, scoping, and quick verification. It is not a vulnerability scanner by default, and it does not replace protocol specific tooling when you need deep application certainty.

Because scanning is active, the boundary is authorization. Use Nmap only on systems you own, operate, or have explicit written permission to test. In most environments, even internal scanning can trigger alerts and incident workflows, so being authorized is not just a legal concern, it is an operational one.

Concept example: a host showing only one open port may not be “secure”, it may be “fronted”. A reverse proxy can expose a single entry point while hiding a large internal surface. Nmap still helps, but you interpret it as “edge exposure”, not “total capability”.

Concept example: if UDP results look empty, that is often normal. UDP is silent by design unless the service chooses to answer, so “no response” is not the same as “no service”. The right conclusion is “I have weak evidence either way”, not “it is closed”.

cliTools.tagline: Map hosts, ports, and services fast, then validate what you think you saw.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: curl is a protocol engine wrapped in a CLI. For HTTP, it constructs a request line, headers, and an optional body, then manages connection setup, redirects, and response parsing. For HTTPS, it also negotiates a TLS session before any HTTP bytes are exchanged.

A request is not just “GET a URL”. It is a sequence: resolve name to an address, open a TCP connection, optionally upgrade to TLS, send the HTTP request, then read the response stream. Failures can happen at any of those layers, and curl is valuable because it lets you see which layer broke without needing a browser UI.

When you enable verbose output, curl reports connection events, negotiation details, and headers. That stream is separate from the response body, which is why you can still capture the body while inspecting what happened on the wire.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: The most common self deception is equating “I got a response” with “the system is healthy”. HTTP status is only a hint. A 200 can carry an application error, a 401 can be expected, and a 500 can be a proxy complaining rather than the origin server failing.

Redirects are another trap. If you follow redirects automatically, you can accidentally test a different host, a different protocol, or a different path than you think. If you do not follow redirects, you can mislabel a working service as broken. The safe mindset is to treat redirects as part of the observed behavior, not as a convenience feature.

TLS errors deserve precise interpretation. A certificate validation failure usually means trust chain issues, hostname mismatch, or an intercepting proxy. It rarely means “TLS is broken” in a general sense. The meaningful question is: broken for which trust store, and for which hostname.

Concept example: two requests to the same URL can produce different results if one includes the right host header and one does not. When you test by IP, you are skipping name based routing, which changes what server you actually reach.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: curl’s power comes from controlling the request shape. You can change method, headers, body encoding, cookies, auth, proxy behavior, and connection timeouts. That turns curl into a lab instrument for reproducing an exact HTTP interaction.

Options cluster into a few mental buckets. Request construction controls what you send. Transport and TLS controls how you connect. Output controls what you capture and where it goes. Debug controls how much you observe about the process. Once you see those categories, curl options stop feeling like a random wall of flags.

There is also a trade between fidelity and convenience. Following redirects and auto decompressing responses makes curl feel “browser like”, but it can hide important behavior. Keeping output minimal is great for scripting, but it can hide the reason for failure. You decide which trade you want for the question you are answering.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: curl fits best when you need repeatable, transparent network requests. It is perfect for API testing, debugging, automation, and validating what a server actually returns. It is not a full browser, so it will not execute JavaScript or model complex client state for you.
Use it only against endpoints you are authorized to test. Even “harmless” requests can trigger rate limits, WAF rules, or incident alerts in production, so the boundary is still scope and permission.

cliTools.tagline: A sharp HTTP and protocol probe for APIs, downloads, and request debugging.

quickPanel.funFact: The name is historically expanded as “Domain Information Groper”, which is exactly what it feels like when you are digging into DNS.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: dig is a DNS message constructor and decoder. It sends a query for a name and record type, then prints back the response sections in a way humans can reason about. Unlike a browser, it does not hide the DNS machinery. It shows you the raw ingredients: answer, authority, additional, flags, and timing.

A normal dig query typically goes to your configured resolver, which may answer from cache, may recurse on your behalf, or may apply policy. When you target a specific server, you are bypassing parts of that behavior and asking a single viewpoint directly, which is crucial for diagnosis.

Trace mode changes the game. Instead of relying on recursion, dig walks the delegation chain using iterative queries, starting at the root and following referrals down to authoritative servers. That reveals where the chain is broken, not just that it is broken.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: The key is separating “what I got back” from “why I got it”. A quick answer could be a warm cache. A slow answer could be a failing upstream or a timeout and retry. The same domain can look stable while your resolver is silently serving stale data.

Pay attention to whether the response is authoritative. An authoritative answer says “this came from a server that claims authority for the zone”. A non authoritative answer can still be correct, but it is mediated by caching and recursion. That distinction matters when you are chasing propagation, hijacks, or misconfigurations.

Concept example: if you query two resolvers and one returns an address and one returns nothing, you have not proven the record exists or not. You have proven the resolvers disagree, which usually points to caching, policy, or split horizon DNS.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: dig is strongest when you treat DNS as a set of layers. There is the naming hierarchy, there are record types, and there are transport behaviors. dig lets you slice along those dimensions: different record types, different servers, different output sections, and different recursion modes.

Flags cluster into: query target selection, output control, and behavior toggles such as trace and DNSSEC related output. The main tradeoff is verbosity versus clarity. Minimal output is great when you are scripting. Full output is what you need when you are debugging how a resolver made a decision.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: dig belongs in every troubleshooting toolkit because DNS is a dependency for almost everything. When an app “cannot connect”, DNS is often the first invisible failure. dig gives you a way to test name resolution without involving the rest of the stack.

Use it responsibly. Querying public resolvers is usually fine, but querying internal zones or enumerating large namespaces can still be sensitive. Stay within scope and treat DNS as operational data, not just trivia.

cliTools.tagline: DNS query tool that shows the resolver’s thinking, not just the final answer.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: nslookup is a DNS query client that talks to a resolver and prints the response in a human friendly way. Underneath, it is still building a DNS question for a name and a type, sending it over the network, and then decoding the server’s reply.

Its most important “under the hood” behavior is which server you are asking. When you use default settings, you are usually talking to a local stub resolver or an enterprise recursive resolver. That server may answer from cache, may recurse to authoritative servers, and may apply filtering or split horizon policies.

In interactive mode, nslookup maintains a current server and current query settings. That statefulness is convenient, but it also makes it easy to forget what context you are in and accidentally compare two answers that were not actually asked the same way.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: DNS is layered, so a single answer is rarely the whole picture. If you receive an address, you still need to ask whether it is authoritative, cached, or policy shaped. If you receive no answer, you need to ask whether it was truly negative, or whether the resolver refused, timed out, or blocked the query.

A practical skepticism: when you troubleshoot “DNS is broken”, assume the first output is telling you only what your chosen resolver believes. That is useful, but it may not match what another network sees. Split DNS and conditional forwarding are common and can make both sides “correct” within their own context.

Concept example: a domain might resolve internally to a private address but externally to a public address. nslookup can reveal that difference quickly, but only if you remember to compare servers, not just repeat the same query.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: nslookup is intentionally narrower than dig. Its strength is speed and availability, especially on Windows systems where it is already present. You can switch servers, choose record types, and perform quick reverse lookups, which covers a large percentage of real world checks.

The tradeoff is precision. The way nslookup prints answers can hide sections and flags that matter when you are diagnosing delegation, DNSSEC, or complex responses. Think of it as a fast probe that tells you where to focus, not as the final word in a DNS investigation.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: nslookup fits in the early stage of troubleshooting: confirm whether a name resolves, compare resolvers, and spot obvious misconfigurations. For deep DNS diagnosis, you usually graduate to dig or packet capture, because those show more of the protocol surface.

Authorized use note: querying DNS servers you control or are allowed to use is fine. Bulk enumeration of third party namespaces or internal domains you do not own crosses ethical and legal lines. Treat DNS like infrastructure, not like a playground.

cliTools.tagline: Quick DNS lookups when you want simple output and fast checks.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: Ping sends ICMP Echo Request messages and waits for Echo Replies. That is a minimal test of reachability at the network layer. It does not involve TCP ports, application protocols, or user level authentication, which is why it is both useful and limited.

Each reply gives you timing information and a few metadata fields such as TTL. Timing reflects the whole path: your host, your local network, the route, and the remote host’s willingness to answer. If any of those components deprioritize ICMP, your measurement becomes a policy measurement rather than a performance measurement.

Because ICMP is handled differently across devices, ping often measures policy as much as physics. Some routers and hosts treat ICMP as low priority background traffic, so the reply you get is sometimes the leftover capacity, not the true latency your TCP flows will experience.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: A ping reply proves that at least one packet made it there and back, but it does not prove the path is stable under load. Low loss at low rate can hide loss under real traffic. Likewise, a long round trip time might be the remote host rate limiting ICMP rather than a slow network.

A missing reply is ambiguous. It can mean the host is down, but it can also mean ICMP is blocked, deprioritized, or filtered on the return path. That is why ping is best interpreted as “evidence of reachability” rather than “proof of failure” when it is silent.

Concept example: a server can respond to ping while its HTTPS service is broken. The network path is fine, but the application stack is not. The inverse can also be true: ICMP is blocked, but the service is reachable on its ports.

When you see packet loss, ask whether it is symmetric. Loss on the way out and loss on the way back look identical in ping output, but they imply different fixes. That is one reason ping is great for detection and alerting, but weaker for pinning down root cause on its own.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: Ping’s knobs mostly change the probe pattern. Count, interval, and packet size affect how hard you test the path and what failure modes you reveal. Some variants can also set the “do not fragment” bit to help detect MTU problems. None of these turn ping into a service checker, they just change the sensitivity of the network layer test.

The core tradeoff is intrusion versus insight. A gentle ping is safe but can miss intermittent problems. Aggressive probing can reveal loss and shaping, but it can also look like noise and trigger alarms in monitored environments.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: Ping is the first tool you use when you need to answer “is there any path at all”. It pairs naturally with traceroute and port specific checks when you need to localize where the problem lives.

Authorized use note: sending a few ICMP probes to systems you own or are permitted to test is normal. Flooding, stress testing, or probing unrelated systems is not. Treat it as a diagnostic instrument, not a weapon.

cliTools.tagline: The simplest latency and reachability signal, with plenty of nuance.

Concluding “ISP issue” from one run. Paths can vary by time and destination.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: Traceroute exploits the IP TTL or hop limit. It sends probes with a low TTL so that the first router expires the packet and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message. Then it raises TTL and repeats, forcing each successive hop to reveal itself by generating the same kind of ICMP response.

The probes themselves can be UDP, ICMP, or TCP depending on platform and options. The key mechanism is consistent: the tool relies on ICMP Time Exceeded from intermediate routers and some form of final response from the destination when the probe finally arrives.

Each hop timing is measured as a round trip for a probe that expired at that hop. It is not a one way delay, and it is not the forwarding delay for your application packets. It is “how long did it take this device to tell me my probe expired”.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: Traceroute output mixes two kinds of truth: routing path and control plane behavior. Routers forward packets in the data plane, but traceroute measures replies from the control plane. A router can forward traffic perfectly while answering traceroute probes slowly, inconsistently, or not at all.

Load balancing complicates interpretation. If the network hashes flows, different probes can be sent along different next hops. That can create the appearance of “branching” paths or fluctuating latency. The right conclusion is often “multiple equal cost paths exist”, not “the network is unstable”.

Concept example: you can see a hop with high latency in the middle of the path, but later hops look normal. That usually means the router is deprioritizing ICMP replies, not that the link is actually slow.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: Traceroute’s capability space is mostly about probe type and resolution. Probe type changes what firewalls and routers will allow through. Resolution and numeric output changes readability. Some variants can also do more advanced probing to keep flows consistent so the path is easier to interpret.

The core trade is visibility versus realism. Probing with something close to your application’s traffic can show a path that matches your real problem, but it may be blocked. Using default probes is often allowed, but it may not represent how your specific service traffic is treated.

Another dimension is how traceroute keeps flows consistent. Some implementations vary ports or identifiers per probe, which can cause load balancers to send different probes down different paths. Tools that keep a stable flow key can produce a cleaner, more interpretable path at the cost of flexibility.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: Traceroute fits when you know “something is slow or failing” and you need to localize where along the path the behavior changes. It is a network layer tool, so you pair it with DNS checks, port checks, and application logs to get a complete picture.

Authorized use note: traceroute is generally low impact, but it is still active probing. Stay within scope, avoid flooding, and remember that some organizations treat repeated traces as suspicious scanning.

cliTools.tagline: See where packets slow down or disappear along the path.

cliTools.name: ss
cliTools.description: Inspect sockets and connection state (modern netstat replacement on Linux).

overview.what: A socket statistics tool for viewing listening ports, active connections, and per-process ownership.
overview.how: Reads kernel socket tables and prints state, addresses, ports, and (optionally) process info, often faster than netstat.
useCases: See what is listening on a port and which process owns it
List established connections and their remote peers
Quickly check if a service bound to the correct interface
overview.use: See what is listening on a port and which process owns it; List established connections and their remote peers; Quickly check if a service bound to the correct interface.

syntaxHelp: Combine protocol flags (-t/-u) with -l to show listeners and -p for process info.
Use a filter to narrow output (ex: 'sport = :443' or 'state established').

examples.explanation: List TCP/UDP sockets with listeners and process ownership (numeric).
Show listening TCP sockets without DNS/service name resolution.
List all TCP/UDP sockets, including non-listening, with processes.
High level socket statistics summary.
Show established TCP connections only (numeric addresses).
Show TCP connections with local source port 443.

notes: Ss reports socket state from the kernel. It is a snapshot that changes moment to moment.
Name resolution can distort speed and clarity. Numeric output is often best for debugging.
Process attribution depends on permissions. Without privilege, some owners stay hidden.
A listening socket is not the same as a working service. The process may still be broken.
proTips: Filter by state to reduce noise. Established and listen views answer different questions.
Use process info when you are hunting “who owns this port”. It turns output into action.
Watch for unexpected binds. Services listening on 0.0.0.0 or :: are exposed broadly.
Pair with logs. Ss tells you what exists, logs tell you why.
commonMistakes: Confusing local and remote columns. It is easy to misread which side owns the port.
Forgetting IPv6. A service can listen on :: and still accept IPv4 via v6 mapping.
Assuming “no connections” means “no traffic”. Short lived connections can come and go fast.
Assuming PID output is complete without privilege. Some details require elevated rights.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: ss is a window into the kernel’s socket tables. Instead of probing the network, it asks the OS what sockets exist, which addresses and ports they are bound to, and what states they are in. That makes it fundamentally different from scanning tools: ss is introspection, not observation.

Because it talks to kernel data structures, ss can surface details that are hard to infer from outside, such as which process owns a socket and which state transitions are happening. It can also reveal when the kernel is carrying lots of connections in transient states, which is often a symptom of load or misbehavior.

ss is part of the iproute2 family and typically queries the kernel through modern interfaces rather than relying on older parsing approaches. That is why it can expose richer state, such as TCP timers and congestion related details, when you ask for them.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: Socket states are easy to misread if you treat them as moral judgments. A large number of connections in a given state is not automatically bad. It becomes meaningful when it is new, growing, or correlated with user visible failures.

Remember the boundary of what ss can prove. It can prove that a process is listening on a port on this machine. It cannot prove that remote clients can reach it. Firewalls, routing, and NAT sit outside the kernel’s local socket table.
Concept example: an app can be listening on 0.0.0.0 but still be unreachable from the internet if a perimeter firewall blocks the port. ss shows local truth, not perimeter truth.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: ss capabilities cluster into: which socket families you look at, which protocol you filter, and how much detail you print. You can focus on listening sockets, established sessions, or summary statistics. You can also filter by address, port, or process to reduce noise.

The tradeoff is between completeness and readability. Dumping everything can be overwhelming. Filtering too hard can make you miss the unusual connection that explains the incident. The skill is choosing a filter that matches your hypothesis without blinding you.

Capabilities also vary by what the kernel exposes. On some systems you can see queue sizes, memory usage, and TCP diagnostics. On others you get a simpler view. The important point is that ss is constrained by local kernel telemetry, not by what the network chooses to reveal.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: ss fits when you are debugging a local system: which service owns this port, why are there so many connections, is the kernel clogged with half closed sockets. It is a perfect companion to external checks like curl or nmap because it shows the internal view that explains the external symptoms.

Authorized use note: ss is local introspection, so the main boundary is system access. Use it on systems you are allowed to administer, and remember that process and connection metadata can be sensitive in shared environments.

cliTools.tagline: Socket snapshot for Linux: who is listening, who is connected, and why.

cliTools.description: List open files and the processes that hold them, including network sockets.

overview.what: A process and file visibility tool: on Unix, everything is a file, including network sockets and devices.
overview.how: Inspects the system's open file tables and prints which processes have which files, sockets, ports, or directories open.

Identify who is keeping a file open (cannot delete/unmount)
List all network connections owned by a process

notes: Lsof maps processes to open files. On busy systems, unfiltered output can be huge.
“File” includes sockets, pipes, and devices. It is broader than most people expect.
Directory scans can be heavy. Recursive modes can get expensive on large trees.
Permissions affect visibility. Some processes will hide details unless you have rights.
proTips: Filter early. Port, PID, user, or path filters make results usable.
Use it for “why can’t I delete this”. Open handles are the usual culprit.
Treat sockets like files. That mental model makes port ownership intuitive.
When debugging binds, disable name resolution. Numeric output is faster and clearer.
commonMistakes: Running it unfiltered and getting lost. Start narrow, then widen.
Mistaking “no output” for “no issue”. You might lack permission to see the owner.
Overusing recursive directory scans on production. It can impact performance.
Forgetting that containers and namespaces change visibility. The host view may differ.
quickPanel.funFact: The name expands to list open files, and on Unix that includes things you do not intuitively think of as files, like network sockets.

sections.title: What the tool is really doing under the hood
paragraphs: lsof correlates process state with the operating system’s open file tables. Every process holds file descriptors that point to kernel objects: regular files, directories, devices, pipes, and sockets. lsof walks those tables and prints a join: process metadata on one side, open handles on the other.

That design is why lsof can answer questions that feel magical: who is using this port, why can’t I unmount this filesystem, what keeps this deleted file consuming disk. It is not guessing. It is reading the kernel’s bookkeeping.

Network related output is a special case of the same mechanism. A listening TCP port is just a socket descriptor. Filtering by network criteria does not change what lsof is doing, it only changes which descriptors it prints.

On Linux, lsof commonly collects this by reading process and descriptor information exposed by the OS, then resolving those kernel objects into something readable. The exact plumbing varies by platform, but the idea is consistent: it is correlating live kernel state, not parsing logs or guessing from symptoms.

sections.title: Interpreting results without fooling yourself
paragraphs: The output is dense, and density invites overconfidence. lsof shows that a process has an open handle. It does not automatically show how important that handle is, or whether it is currently active. A process can keep a file open for hours without touching it again.

Be careful with the meaning of this port is used by PID X. In containerized and multi namespace environments, the same port number can exist in different namespaces. lsof shows what it can see from the namespace and privileges you are in, which might be a partial truth.
Concept example: a log file may be deleted, but disk usage does not drop because a process still holds the descriptor. lsof can reveal that hidden link between deleted and still consuming space.

Also watch for handles that point to “deleted” paths. The filesystem entry is gone, but the inode can stay allocated while the process keeps the descriptor open. That is why disk usage and file listings can disagree until the process releases the handle.

sections.title: The shape of the tool’s capabilities
paragraphs: lsof is all about selection and projection. Selection decides which processes and which kinds of files you care about: user, PID, file path, network sockets, or a mix. Projection decides how verbose the output is. Those are the two axes that make it either a scalpel or a firehose.

The main tradeoff is cost. Narrow queries are fast. Wide queries can be expensive because lsof must inspect many processes and many descriptors. That cost is not just time, it can be measurable load on a busy system. In incident response, that matters.

sections.title: Context and boundaries
paragraphs: lsof fits when your question is who owns the resource. It complements ss and netstat style tools by tying sockets to processes, and it complements filesystem tools by tying paths to open handles.

Authorized use note: lsof reveals process names, users, open paths, and network endpoints. On shared systems that can be sensitive. Use it only where you have admin authority, and be intentional about what you capture and share in reports.

cliTools.tagline: See which process holds a file, port, or directory open.

cliTools.name: Lynis
cliTools.description: Run a structured local security audit and get prioritized hardening recommendations.

overview.what: Lynis is a local security auditing tool that reviews your system configuration, installed software, and security controls. It highlights weaknesses, missing hardening steps, and potential misconfigurations in areas like authentication, logging, networking, and file permissions.
overview.how: Lynis runs a large set of checks grouped by category and produces two outputs: a log with technical details and a report that summarizes warnings and suggestions. You can run it interactively, in quick mode, or as a scheduled run to track improvements over time.
useCases: Baseline a new server build before it goes live.
Re audit after major changes, patch cycles, or configuration hardening.
Support compliance style reviews by keeping reports and comparing audits over time.

examples.explanation: Run a full local audit with maximum coverage (recommended for your baseline).

See available scan modes and common options directly from the installed version.

notes: Run with sudo for the most complete results. Without elevated privileges, some checks will be skipped.
Treat the output as guidance, not a verdict. Suggestions should be validated against your threat model and operational needs.
Keep reports for comparison. The real value shows up when you can prove that hardening is improving over time.
proTips: Start with quick mode for frequent runs, then do a full run after major changes.
Use a profile to suppress noise and focus on controls you actually plan to enforce.
Turn key findings into repeatable hardening tasks, then re run Lynis to confirm closure.
commonMistakes: Trying to fix everything at once. Prioritize high impact warnings first.
Running only once and forgetting it. Lynis is most useful when used as a recurring checkpoint.
Ignoring context. A hardening suggestion can be correct in general but wrong for your workload.
quickPanel.funFact: Lynis writes both a detailed log and a separate report so you can keep a clean summary while still retaining technical evidence.

sections.title: How Lynis audits a system
paragraphs: Lynis performs a series of categorized tests that inspect configuration files, package settings, permissions, kernel parameters, and security controls. The tests are designed to be read only, so the tool does not harden the system for you, it explains what it found and what to consider changing.

Because it is local, Lynis can correlate details that remote scanners often miss, such as local authentication policies, file ownership patterns, sudo configuration, and logging and auditing coverage. This makes it a strong companion to network scanning and vulnerability scanning.

The audit is more complete when you run as root, since privileged access allows Lynis to inspect restricted files and system settings. If you must run unprivileged, treat the results as partial and focus on what it can still verify safely.

sections.title: Reports, warnings, and the hardening index
paragraphs: Lynis produces a log with raw findings and a report file that summarizes warnings and suggestions. The report is the part you typically store for baselining and review meetings, while the log is what you consult when you need technical details behind a finding.

Warnings are usually higher urgency and are good candidates for immediate triage. Suggestions can range from quick wins to deeper architecture choices. A practical workflow is to convert the highest value items into tasks, apply changes in a controlled way, and then re run Lynis to validate impact.

Many environments use the hardening index as a simple trend indicator. It is not a compliance score, but it is useful to show that security posture is improving when you combine it with evidence from the report files.

sections.title: Making Lynis actionable
paragraphs: The biggest jump in value comes when you treat Lynis output as a backlog. Pick a small number of improvements, implement them, and verify. This turns the audit from a one time report into a continuous hardening loop.
Profiles help reduce noise. If a recommendation is intentionally not applicable, capture that decision in a profile so future runs stay focused and consistent across systems.

When working across fleets, run Lynis on representative hosts first. Use the results to define a baseline configuration, then standardize and automate the hardening steps through your configuration management tools.

sections.title: Automation and safe recurring runs
paragraphs: For scheduled audits, cronjob mode is designed for non interactive execution. Combine it with a stable report path and a log management approach so reports can be collected or compared centrally.
Be mindful of sensitive output. Audit logs and reports can contain system information that you would not want broadly accessible. Store them with appropriate permissions and retention policies.
A practical cadence is frequent quick runs plus deeper full audits after patching, configuration changes, or major upgrades. This keeps the signal high and the effort predictable.

Use --profile <file> to tune checks and reporting to your environment.

cliTools.name: auditd
cliTools.description: Collect and query tamper resistant audit logs for authentication, file access, and admin activity.

overview.what: auditd is the Linux Audit daemon that records security relevant events from the kernel audit framework. It is commonly used to track authentication activity, privilege use, file integrity sensitive paths, and policy enforced monitoring for compliance.
overview.how: Rules define what gets logged. The kernel generates audit events, auditd writes them to /var/log/audit/audit.log, and tools like auditctl, ausearch, and aureport help you manage rules and turn raw events into readable answers.
useCases: Detect changes to critical files such as passwd, sudoers, or SSH configuration.
Create audit trails for privileged commands and admin actions.
Generate periodic audit reports to support investigations and compliance reviews.

examples.explanation: Confirm what rules are currently active. Do this before adding more rules.

Find events for the sudoers change key and interpret fields into readable output.
Produce a readable report of login activity in a time window.
Verify the daemon is running and logs are being written.

notes: Keep rules focused. Audit volume grows quickly and can create noise and performance impact.
Keys are essential. Tag your rules with keys so you can search reliably during incidents.
Persist rules in files, not only in memory. In memory rules set via auditctl can be lost after reboot.
proTips: Start with a small set of high value watches, then iterate based on what you actually investigate.
Use ausearch with -i when presenting results to humans and raw mode when feeding scripts.
Protect audit logs with strict permissions and a clear retention plan so the trail stays trustworthy.
commonMistakes: Monitoring too broadly, for example entire filesystems, which produces unusable volumes of logs.
Forgetting to persist rules, causing monitoring to silently disappear after reboots or service restarts.
Skipping filters like auid or success, which can inflate noise and hide meaningful events.
quickPanel.funFact: Audit events are generated by the kernel, which is one reason audit trails can be more reliable than application only logging.

sections.title: Mental model: from syscall to audit.log
paragraphs: The Linux Audit framework is built into the kernel. When a monitored action happens, such as a syscall you have rules for, the kernel emits an audit event with fields that describe who did what, from where, and whether it succeeded.
auditd receives those events and writes them to /var/log/audit/audit.log. That log is structured text, which is great for integrity and parsing but not always pleasant to read directly.

This is why the ecosystem includes query tools. ausearch helps you filter events by time, user, key, or many other attributes. aureport turns collections of events into summary reports you can hand to a reviewer.

sections.title: Rule types: watch rules and syscall rules
paragraphs: Watch rules (the -w style) are the easiest entry point. You monitor a file or directory path and select which permission types to record. They are perfect for tracking changes to configuration files and other high value assets.

Syscall rules (the -a always,exit style) are more flexible and powerful. You can target syscalls like open or execve and then filter by user IDs, executables, success or failure, and more. This is how you create precise detection for behavior, not just a file path.

Keys glue everything together. When you assign -k to a rule, every matching event carries that tag, making incident response far faster because you can search by intent, not by guessing which raw fields will match.

sections.title: Searching and reporting that actually answers questions
paragraphs: During investigations, start from a key or a time window. Use ausearch to narrow the log to the events you care about, then add interpretation so numeric IDs become usernames and paths become readable.
For recurring reviews, aureport is often the better interface. Login reports, authentication reports, and executable summaries can quickly tell you what changed or what stood out in a given period.
A good practice is to test your rules. Trigger the behavior in a controlled way, confirm the events appear, and then document the key and expected output so others can repeat the process.

sections.title: Operational hygiene: performance, retention, and integrity
paragraphs: Audit is powerful, but it is not free. High volume rule sets can increase CPU usage and I O, and they can fill disks. Tune rules deliberately and monitor both event rate and log growth.

Configuration in /etc/audit/auditd.conf controls behavior such as log rotation and what to do when disk space is low. Those settings matter, because losing the audit trail during an incident defeats the point.
Treat audit data as evidence. Restrict access, ship copies to a centralized log system if possible, and define retention and rotation so you can answer questions weeks or months later.

cliTools.name: ClamAV
cliTools.description: Scan files and directories for malware using signatures, with options for daemon mode and updates.

overview.what: ClamAV is an open source antivirus engine commonly used on Unix like systems. It focuses on file based malware detection using signature databases and can be used for on demand scans, scheduled scans, or integrated scanning in services that handle untrusted files.
overview.how: Use freshclam to keep virus signatures up to date. For scanning, you can run clamscan as a standalone scanner, or run the clamd daemon and use clamdscan for faster repeated scans. The scanning behavior and logging can be tuned with configuration and command options.
useCases: Scan uploads in web apps or file shares before storing or distributing content.
Run scheduled filesystem scans to reduce dwell time for commodity malware.
Integrate with mail gateways and content pipelines that need automated scanning.

examples.explanation: Update signatures before scanning so results reflect the latest database.
Recursively scan a directory and show only infected findings.
Scan a sensitive directory and keep a log for audit trails.
Quarantine infected files by moving them to a controlled directory.
Use the clamd daemon for faster scans on larger directories (requires clamd running).

notes: Signature scanning is great for known malware, but it will not catch everything. Use defense in depth with least privilege and monitoring.
Always keep signatures updated. Outdated databases are a common reason for missed detections.
Prefer quarantine (move or copy) over delete until you are confident in your false positive handling.
proTips: Exclude virtual filesystems like proc and sys and other noisy paths in large scans.
Use clamd for repeated scanning workloads. It avoids reloading signatures for every run.
Log to a dedicated path and include scan cadence in your operational playbook.
commonMistakes: Running long recursive scans without exclusions, which wastes time and produces irrelevant errors.
Deleting infected files immediately, which can destroy evidence or break systems if a false positive occurs.
Assuming one clean scan proves safety. Scans are a point in time view.
quickPanel.funFact: ClamAV is widely used as an engine inside other products, especially where automated scanning of untrusted files is needed.

sections.title: What ClamAV can and cannot do well
paragraphs: ClamAV is primarily a signature based malware scanner. It is very effective for detecting known threats and commodity malware families when the signature database is current.
It is not an endpoint protection suite with behavior based prevention by default. Treat it as one layer in a larger control set that includes patching, hardening, least privilege, and logging.
In practice, ClamAV shines in pipelines: file upload scanning, mail scanning, and server side hygiene checks where you want an automated verdict with a clear audit trail.

sections.title: Standalone scanning versus daemon mode
paragraphs: clamscan runs as a standalone process. It is simple and great for one off checks, but it must load signature databases each run, which can be slow for repeated workloads.

clamd runs as a long lived daemon that keeps signatures in memory and can scan in parallel. clamdscan is the client that sends scan requests to the daemon. This approach is usually faster for large directories or frequent scans.
If you deploy clamd, treat the daemon like a service: define clear sockets, permissions, and logging, and make sure your update workflow keeps signatures current without interrupting critical scans.

sections.title: Signature updates and handling false positives
paragraphs: freshclam updates the official signature databases. In production, schedule updates and monitor for failures, because a silent update problem can leave you behind for weeks.
Quarantine workflows matter. Moving or copying infected files to a dedicated directory allows you to investigate, validate, and restore if it turns out to be a false positive.

If you see repeated false positives in known benign files, document the pattern and decide how to handle it. Sometimes exclusion rules are appropriate, but exclusions should be tightly scoped and reviewed.

sections.title: Operational patterns for servers and pipelines
paragraphs: For filesystem scanning, define what success looks like: which paths are in scope, which are excluded, where logs go, and what happens on detection. Without this, scans become noise.

For application pipelines, scan before the file is trusted. For example, scan on upload and again before distributing or executing content. This reduces risk even when users supply untrusted payloads.
Combine scanning results with monitoring. A scan result alone does not explain how a file arrived, who touched it, or what it did. That context comes from logging, auditing, and access controls.

guiTools.name: Wireshark
guiTools.description: Packet capture and protocol analyzer for inspecting network traffic.

overview.what: A network protocol analyzer for reading what actually happened on the wire. You can capture live traffic from a chosen interface or open an existing PCAP and then inspect each layer of every packet (Ethernet, IP, TCP/UDP, TLS, HTTP, DNS and many more) with timestamps, conversations, and flow context.
overview.how: Wireshark ingests packets from a live interface or a PCAP file and runs them through protocol dissectors that decode fields at each layer. Capture filters (BPF) control which packets are recorded; display filters work after the fact on decoded fields to show or hide what you care about. With reassembly and stream following, you can reconstruct conversations and reason across packets rather than reading them one by one.
useCases: Troubleshoot latency, retransmissions, and connection resets
Verify DNS queries, HTTP requests, and TLS handshakes
Investigate suspicious traffic in a PCAP from an incident

Protocol decoding with deep per-field inspection

Many environments require admin/root privileges to capture from interfaces.

Timing is evidence. Look at retransmissions, out-of-order segments, and RTT.

commonMistakes: Using a display filter expecting it to reduce capture size.
Reading TCP like single packets; always reason in streams.
Ignoring capture vantage point (SPAN, tap, client, server) which changes truth.
Forgetting to disable name resolution when you need speed and clarity.
quickPanel.whatGoodLooksLike: You can narrate a flow from handshake to teardown with 2–3 packets that prove each claim.

sections.title: Capture filters versus display filters: decide where you want to pay the cost
paragraphs: Wireshark gives you two fundamentally different filtering levers. Capture filters decide what gets collected in the first place. Display filters decide what you see and analyze after the packets are already captured.

Capture filters are powerful when you need to reduce volume on a busy link, or when you are collecting with limited disk and you already know what traffic you want. The tradeoff is that you cannot get back what you never captured. If you guess wrong, you may have to re capture.

Display filters are the workhorse for investigation. They let you iterate quickly, pivot between hypotheses, and refine your view as you learn more. A strong habit is to capture broadly when you can, then use display filters to narrow down in a disciplined way.

sections.title: Dissection and streams: how Wireshark turns packets into meaning
paragraphs: Wireshark is not just showing bytes. It is dissecting protocols and mapping fields into a structured model. That model is what makes filtering and searching possible, because you can filter on protocol fields instead of raw offsets.

When troubleshooting, it is often more useful to think in conversations and streams than in individual packets. Features like following a TCP stream help you reconstruct application layer exchanges, validate assumptions about request and response order, and spot where a conversation goes off the rails.

Be mindful of reassembly and encryption. Reassembly can change what you see at the application layer, and encryption can hide payloads entirely. In those cases, metadata, timing, sizes, and handshake details become the clues you use.

sections.title: A repeatable investigation loop that scales
paragraphs: A practical workflow is: start wide, identify the talking parties, then narrow. Use high level statistics to see which protocols dominate and which endpoints are most active. Then drill into a single conversation or a small set of flows.

As you narrow, validate each step. If you suspect a specific host, confirm it appears in endpoints or conversations. If you suspect a specific protocol behavior, confirm it in the protocol tree and then filter down to the exact fields that prove or disprove the hypothesis.
This approach keeps you from getting lost in packet noise and makes your analysis auditable: each filter you apply represents a decision you can explain.

sections.title: Statistics are not a side feature: they are your compass
paragraphs: Wireshark’s statistics views help you build intuition fast. Protocol hierarchy gives you a quick baseline of what is present. Conversations and endpoints show who is driving the traffic. I O graphs and timing views help you align events in time and spot bursts, stalls, and retransmission patterns.

When you are diagnosing performance issues, you often do not need to look at payloads at all. You need to understand timing, resets, retransmissions, window behavior, and where delays appear. Statistics plus targeted packet views are the fastest path.

sections.title: When you outgrow the GUI: bring in TShark and automation
paragraphs: The Wireshark ecosystem includes command line tooling for repeatable work. TShark lets you capture or read pcap files and extract fields, apply filters, and generate summaries in scripts. This is how you scale analysis beyond a single workstation.

A good pattern is: explore interactively in Wireshark to find the exact display filter and the exact fields you need, then codify that in TShark for repeatable extraction. That way the GUI becomes your research environment and automation becomes your production workflow.

guiTools.name: Burp Suite
guiTools.description: Web security testing platform for intercepting and analyzing HTTP(S) traffic.

overview.what: An intercepting proxy workflow for web testing. Burp sits between your browser and the application so you can observe, modify, and replay HTTP(S) and WebSocket traffic while organizing targets and findings in one place.
overview.how: Burp runs a local proxy and routes your browser’s requests through it. You can intercept and edit requests and responses, then send items to Repeater for controlled manual testing or to Intruder for automated payload exploration. With the Burp CA installed in your browser, HTTPS traffic is decrypted inside your testing scope for inspection.

Replay and modify requests to test authorization, input handling, and logic
Organize targets and keep only in-scope traffic

Install Burp's CA certificate if you need to inspect HTTPS
Set target scope so Burp highlights only the sites you care about
Use Proxy to intercept and modify requests
Send requests to Repeater for manual testing and to Intruder for automation

Repeater for manual request iteration
Intruder for automated payload testing (capabilities vary by edition)
quickSetup: Open Burp → Proxy tab → confirm a listener is running on 127.0.0.1:8080
Use 'Open Browser' in Burp, or configure your browser to use Burp as an HTTP proxy
Install Burp's CA certificate in the browser to decrypt HTTPS (only for your own testing)

Toggle Intercept on/off in Proxy → Intercept
Send requests to Repeater for manual testing
Add targets to Scope to focus your work
Filter Proxy history to in-scope only
Send to Intruder for safe, scoped payload iteration
Add comments/highlights to important items
Save the project frequently (burp project file)

You need to see exactly what the browser sends and receives
You want to reproduce a bug or verify a security control

If HTTPS looks broken, the CA certificate usually isn't installed or proxy settings are wrong.
Scope controls noise. Keeping targets in-scope prevents accidental testing out of bounds.

Mark interesting requests with comments and highlights to build your story.
Filter Proxy history to in-scope before searching.
