Forgetting to turn Intercept off and wondering why pages hang.
Assuming a 200 means success; read the response body.
quickPanel.whatGoodLooksLike: You can show a minimal request that reproduces the issue, explain why it works, and list the header or parameter that controls it.

sections.title: Burp as an instrumentation layer for web applications
paragraphs: Burp Suite is easiest to use when you treat it as a lens and a control surface for HTTP and WebSocket traffic. By placing Burp between your browser and the target, you can observe what the application actually sends and receives, not what you assume it sends and receives.

Intercepting requests and responses is not just for changing parameters. It is a way to learn the application’s state transitions, how it uses cookies and headers, and which requests are security critical. That understanding is what makes later testing efficient instead of random.

sections.title: Manual testing loop: Proxy, Target, Repeater
paragraphs: A high signal workflow is to browse the target through Burp, then use the Target site map and history views to organize what you discovered. The site map represents Burp’s accumulated knowledge of the application, collected from your browsing and other tools.

Once you have an interesting request, move it into Repeater. Repeater is where you do controlled experimentation: adjust one variable at a time, resend, and observe the response. This is how you confirm behavior, reproduce issues, and understand how the server validates input.

sections.title: Sessions and authentication: staying logged in on purpose
paragraphs: Many testing workflows fail because the tool silently falls out of an authenticated session. Burp provides session handling functionality so you can define rules for maintaining a valid session, manage cookies, and use macros to refresh authentication when needed.

The key is to define what “logged in” looks like, then automate the recovery path. When configured correctly, your manual testing and any automated steps will keep consistent access to authenticated areas, which dramatically improves coverage and reduces false negatives.

sections.title: Out of band detection and Burp Collaborator
paragraphs: Some vulnerabilities do not show up in the immediate HTTP response. They trigger server side interactions such as DNS lookups or HTTP callbacks. Burp Collaborator is designed to detect those out of band interactions and is used by Burp’s scanning features and extensions where available.

The practical value is confirmation. When you see an interaction in Collaborator, you have evidence that a payload caused an external effect, which is often stronger than a subtle difference in an on page response.

sections.title: Make Burp work like a lab notebook
paragraphs: Burp becomes far more effective when you keep it organized. Define target scope early so history and tasks do not fill with unrelated traffic. Use filtering to focus on status codes, parameterized endpoints, or specific content types when you triage.

Treat each finding as a reproducible experiment. Keep the exact request that demonstrates the issue, the minimal change that triggers it, and the evidence in the response. That discipline turns a pile of traffic into actionable security work.

guiTools.name: OWASP ZAP
guiTools.description: Open source web application security testing tool for intercepting, exploring, and scanning HTTP and WebSocket traffic.

overview.what: OWASP ZAP is a desktop proxy and scanner for web application security testing. It sits between your browser and a target application, records traffic, and lets you inspect, modify, and replay requests. On top of that, it can crawl an application and run passive and active checks to help you discover common security issues.
overview.how: In practice, ZAP works best when you combine manual exploration with controlled automation. You explore the app through ZAP’s proxy, define what is in scope, and let passive scanning analyze the traffic you generate. Then you crawl the target (Spider and, for modern JS apps, AJAX Spider) to expand coverage. Finally, you run active scanning against the confirmed in scope targets and review findings in context of the actual requests, responses, and evidence ZAP captured.
useCases: Developer friendly DAST checks during development and in CI pipelines using automation plans.
Learning web app security by observing real traffic and understanding where issues come from.
Security testing on staging environments, including authenticated areas with session handling configured.

workflow: Set your scope: define the target domain(s) and what should be excluded (logouts, destructive endpoints, third party services).
Proxy your browser through ZAP and browse the application normally to generate realistic traffic.
Review the Sites tree and History to confirm coverage, then enable or tune passive scan rules as needed.
Crawl for coverage: run Spider for classic apps and AJAX Spider for JS heavy apps; combine both when needed.
Configure authentication and session management if the app requires login, then verify you can stay authenticated while crawling.
Run Active Scan only against in scope targets you have permission to test, then validate findings by reproducing requests and checking evidence.
Export reports or save the session and triage issues with developers using request/response details.
features: Intercepting proxy for HTTP and WebSocket traffic, with request editing and replay driven workflows.
Passive scanning that analyzes proxied traffic without attacking the target.
Spider and AJAX Spider crawling to discover content, endpoints, and parameters.
Active scanning to probe for vulnerabilities against confirmed in scope targets.
Contexts, users, and session management to support authenticated testing.
Automation Framework for repeatable scans using a single plan file and job based workflows.

quickActions: Quick Start: run an Automated Scan against a URL when you need a fast first pass.
Spider and AJAX Spider: expand coverage before scanning.
Active Scan: attack only what is in scope and permitted.
Context setup: define scope, authentication, and session handling for repeatability.
commonFilters: Scope only: focus views and results on what you actually own and intend to test.
History and alerts filters: narrow by URL, status code, type, and risk level when triaging.
Exclude noisy paths: logouts, health checks, analytics, and large static asset trees.
exports: Generate a report for stakeholders, including evidence and affected URLs.
Export alerts to integrate with issue tracking or to compare between runs.
Save the session to preserve history, sites tree, and scan results for later review.

when: You need an open source, approachable web app testing tool that supports both manual and automated workflows.
You want to learn how web requests, responses, cookies, and headers relate to common vulnerabilities.
You are building a repeatable DAST check in CI and want a plan driven approach.
notes: Run active scans only on targets you are authorized to test, and start on staging environments.
Coverage matters more than button clicking. Crawl and explore first, scan second.
If the app is authenticated, spend time on Context, users, and session management. It pays off immediately.
Think in phases: scope, explore, crawl, scan, validate.
Passive scan is low risk, active scan is intrusive and can break things.
proTips: Combine Spider and AJAX Spider for modern apps. One crawler rarely covers everything.
Treat Context configuration like code: keep it stable and reuse it through automation plans.
commonMistakes: Scanning without a defined scope and getting overwhelmed by third party noise.
Running active scan before you have coverage, which leads to false confidence.
Ignoring authentication setup and accidentally testing only the login page.

sections.title: The mental model: proxy first, scanner second
paragraphs: ZAP is easiest to understand if you treat it as two systems that work together. The first is the proxy, which captures and organizes traffic as you use the application. The second is a set of analysis and scanning engines that operate on that captured traffic or on URLs discovered during crawling.

If you skip the proxy mindset and jump straight to scanning, you lose context. You will not know whether a finding is actually reachable, whether it depends on a specific session state, or whether it is being triggered by a third party page you do not own. The proxy view is what turns raw alerts into evidence that developers can reproduce.

A practical habit is to keep asking: “Do I understand the request that caused this?” If the answer is no, go back to History, inspect the request and response, and only then decide whether the alert is a real issue or just noise.

sections.title: Passive scanning versus active scanning
paragraphs: Passive scanning inspects the traffic you generate while browsing or replaying requests. It does not attack the application. This makes it a safe way to learn and a low risk way to run checks continuously during development.

Active scanning is the opposite: ZAP actively sends payloads and variations to try to trigger vulnerabilities. It can cause side effects, load, or unexpected behavior. The point is not to “scan everything”, but to scan what you have verified is in scope, reachable, and stable enough to test.

A good workflow is to use passive results as a compass. If passive scan flags missing security headers, insecure cookies, or suspicious parameters, you can prioritize where deeper manual testing and controlled active scanning will produce the best signal.

sections.title: Coverage is everything: Spider and AJAX Spider
paragraphs: Most disappointing scan results are coverage problems, not scanner problems. If ZAP never sees a page, a parameter, or a workflow, it cannot analyze it. That is why crawling is a first class skill in web app testing.

ZAP’s classic Spider is great for traditional link based sites. Modern applications often build routes and content dynamically in JavaScript, which is why ZAP also has an AJAX Spider add on that drives a browser based crawler. Combining the two often gives the best results: the Spider gets the obvious content fast, while the AJAX Spider explores dynamic states.

Treat crawling outputs as data. Look at what endpoints were discovered, which were not, and what should be excluded. Only after you trust your discovered attack surface should you spend time on active scanning and alert triage.

sections.title: Contexts, authentication, and session handling
paragraphs: Authenticated scanning is where tools either become valuable or become frustrating. ZAP uses Contexts to define scope, users, authentication method, and session management. The goal is to make “being logged in” a repeatable configuration rather than a manual ritual.

Session management determines how ZAP tracks whether it is still authenticated, typically via cookies or HTTP auth, and it can be extended with scripts when applications use custom mechanisms. Once configured, you should validate it by browsing and crawling for a while and verifying that the requests remain in an authenticated state.

This is also where you control safety. By excluding logout links, destructive actions, and admin only flows from a Context, you reduce the chance that crawling or scanning triggers accidental changes while still allowing meaningful coverage.

sections.title: Automation Framework: repeatable scans as a plan
paragraphs: For non trivial testing, repeatability matters. ZAP’s Automation Framework lets you define a sequence of jobs such as spidering and active scanning in a single plan file. The plan captures what is in scope, how authentication works, and what scanning steps to run so results are comparable between runs.

A strong pattern is “desktop to automate”. Configure and validate the Context and authentication in the GUI first, then export that setup into an automation plan and run it in CI. That way, automation inherits a configuration you already proved works.

If you treat the plan as part of your security pipeline, you can start small with passive checks and crawling, then add active scan jobs for specific contexts once the environment and exclusions are mature.

detectionTool.name: Suricata
detectionTool.desc: Inspect network traffic for threats using an IDS engine with rules, logs, and EVE JSON telemetry.
quickSetup: Set HOME_NET and your capture method in /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml so the engine understands what is internal and which interface(s) to monitor.
Fetch the default rule set with sudo suricata-update, then confirm rules are installed under /var/lib/suricata/rules.
Restart the service (sudo systemctl restart suricata) and verify Suricata starts cleanly by checking /var/log/suricata/suricata.log.
Confirm packets are being processed by tailing /var/log/suricata/stats.log and looking for growing counters (processed packets, decoded protocols, drops).
Validate your configuration and rules before deep tuning: sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml.
Trigger a known test alert, then watch fast.log and EVE JSON to confirm you get both human readable alerts and structured events.
actions: Show build details and enabled capture features: sudo suricata --build-info
Test configuration and rule loading: sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
Run on an interface in IDS mode: sudo suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -i eth0
Daemonize when running from a terminal: sudo suricata -D -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -i eth0
Replay a capture for offline triage: sudo suricata -r traffic.pcap -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
Keep processing a directory of PCAPs as files arrive: sudo suricata -r /pcaps --pcap-file-continuous -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml
Filter alert events from EVE JSON: sudo tail -f /var/log/suricata/eve.json | jq 'select(.event_type=="alert")'
Reload rules without restarting (socket): sudo suricatasc -c reload-rules
Reload rules without restarting (signal): sudo kill -USR2 $(pidof suricata)
Override a simple setting at runtime: sudo suricata --set default-log-dir=/var/tmp -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -i eth0
detectionTool.description: IDS/IPS engine for inspecting network traffic with rules and rich JSON logging.

overview.what: Suricata is an open source intrusion detection and prevention engine that inspects network traffic in real time. It raises alerts using signature rules and can also produce rich network telemetry as structured events.
overview.how: Packets are captured from an interface or replayed from PCAP, decoded into protocol and flow records, then evaluated against rule sets. Output is written to alert logs and to EVE JSON so events can be filtered, shipped to a SIEM, and correlated with other data sources.
useCases: Detect known exploits, malware command and control patterns, and suspicious scanning using signatures.
Generate DNS, HTTP, TLS, file, and flow telemetry for threat hunting and incident response.
Run retrospective analysis on packet captures to confirm or triage an incident quickly.

features: Signature based detection with rule sets that can be updated and managed.
Rich telemetry via EVE JSON for alerts, DNS, HTTP, TLS, files, and statistics.
Multiple output formats including fast.log and structured JSON for automation.
Configurable capture and performance settings for low to high throughput environments.
workflow: Capture packets from an interface or pcap input and decode protocols and flows.
Match traffic against signature rules and track state across sessions.
Write alerts and metadata to log outputs that you can feed into SIEM or analysis tooling.
Tune rules and configuration to reduce noise and improve signal for your environment.
when: You want IDS visibility and structured logs from network traffic
You are learning detection engineering or blue team triage
You need to confirm whether a pattern is visible in network telemetry
notes: The best results come from tuning HOME_NET and rule selection. Default rule sets are useful, but every network needs tuning to reduce false positives.
Treat Suricata output as telemetry. Alerts are one output, but protocol metadata is often the real hunting gold.
Start simple, then scale. Verify capture and logging first, then add performance tuning and integrations.
detectionTool.tagline: Network threat detection with signatures and rich structured event output.

notes: Begin with visibility. Confirm packets are being processed and logs are moving before chasing alerts.
Use EVE JSON for workflows that need automation, correlation, and long term analytics.
Rule tuning is ongoing. Plan time for triage, suppression, and adding environment specific detection.
proTips: Use suricata-update regularly so rules stay current, and track changes in a controlled way.
Tail stats.log when tuning performance. Dropped packets or decode failures show up there early.
Send EVE JSON into a central log platform so you can correlate Suricata with host logs and identity data.
commonMistakes: Leaving HOME_NET too broad or too narrow, which creates noise or missed detection.
Relying only on fast.log. You lose a lot of useful context compared to EVE JSON.
Enabling every rule without tuning, leading to alert fatigue and poor signal to noise.
quickPanel.funFact: Suricata can output both high level alerts and low level protocol metadata, which makes it useful for both detection and network visibility.

sections.title: From packets to events
paragraphs: Suricata starts with packet capture. It ingests traffic from a live interface or from recorded pcaps, then decodes protocols and tracks flows so it can reason about sessions instead of isolated packets.

Detection rules operate on this decoded context. Rules can match on payload content, protocol fields, flow direction, and other attributes, which allows meaningful alerts like a specific exploit attempt or suspicious command and control pattern.

In parallel, Suricata can emit protocol metadata. Even when no signature triggers, those events give you visibility into what happened on the wire, which is essential for threat hunting and incident timelines.

sections.title: Rules, updates, and tuning
paragraphs: Rule sets are the detection brain. The default experience often starts with ET Open rules, then evolves into a curated selection based on your environment and your threat model.

suricata-update helps fetch and manage rule sources and keeps the deployed rules consistent with your configuration. Updates should be treated like software changes: test, deploy, and monitor for new noise.
Tuning is where value is created. Suppress known benign patterns, disable irrelevant categories, and add custom rules for your assets. This turns generic IDS into environment specific detection.

sections.title: Understanding outputs: fast.log versus EVE JSON
paragraphs: fast.log is a human friendly alert log. It is great for quick verification and hands on testing, but it is not ideal for automation because it is not strongly structured.

EVE JSON is structured event output. It can include alerts, protocol records, file events, and statistics. Because it is JSON, you can filter and transform it with tools like jq and ship it to SIEM platforms with minimal friction.
A practical approach is to use fast.log for immediate debugging and EVE JSON for everything you want to retain, correlate, and analyze at scale.

sections.title: Deployment patterns and performance basics
paragraphs: Most teams start in IDS mode on a single interface with default logging, then expand into multiple sensors, dedicated capture hardware, or inline IPS patterns depending on needs and risk tolerance.
Performance is about capture reliability. Monitor packet drops, thread behavior, and decode stats. If you miss packets, you miss detection. stats.log and Suricata logs are your early warning signals.
Keep configurations explicit. Document HOME_NET, rule sources, and output settings, and treat changes as part of your normal change management so detection stays stable and explainable.

detectionTools.name: Zeek
detectionTools.desc: Protocol aware network analysis engine that generates structured telemetry (logs) and supports custom detections through an event driven scripting language.
detectionTools.description: Network security monitor that analyzes traffic and produces rich, protocol aware logs plus an event driven scripting layer for custom detections.

overview.what: Zeek observes network traffic and extracts protocol metadata into structured logs such as connections, DNS, HTTP, TLS, and files. Instead of focusing on signatures, it builds high quality telemetry that helps you answer “who talked to whom, when, and how” across many protocols.
overview.how: Zeek parses traffic with protocol analyzers. As it recognizes protocol elements, it raises events into its scripting layer and writes logs via its logging framework. You can extend behavior with scripts and packages: add fields, create new logs, raise notices, enrich with threat intel feeds, and tune what Zeek considers interesting.
useCases: Incident response and threat hunting by pivoting through conn, dns, http, ssl, files, and notice logs.
Building detections that rely on protocol behavior rather than brittle payload signatures.
Creating long term network baselines and anomaly investigations using consistent, query friendly logs.

quickSetup: Place Zeek on a sensor that can see the traffic you care about (SPAN, TAP, or host based capture).
Start with default scripts and confirm core logs (conn, dns, http, ssl, notice) are being generated.
Choose an output format and log rotation strategy that fits your pipeline (text or JSON, rotation intervals).
Integrate with your SIEM or data lake, then add packages or custom scripts for your environment.
actions: Start with conn.log to map connections, then pivot into protocol specific logs like dns.log and http.log.
Raise notices for suspicious behaviors and route them to your alerting pipeline.
Feed threat intelligence indicators into the Intel framework for matching against traffic.
Enable file analysis to extract metadata and hashes from transferred files.
Tune logging by filtering logs, adding fields that matter, and adjusting rotation and retention.
features: Protocol aware logs for many common network protocols, designed for hunting and incident response.
Event driven scripting language to customize detections and extend Zeek’s outputs.
Logging framework with flexible rotation, filtering, and optional post processing.
Notice framework to turn script logic into actionable, structured alerts.
Intelligence framework for indicator ingestion and matching.
File analysis framework for metadata extraction across supported protocols.
Package manager (zkg) to install and manage third party scripts and plugins.
workflow: Collect traffic on the sensor and validate that timestamps, interfaces, and capture visibility are correct.
Establish a baseline: review conn.log plus a small set of protocol logs (dns, http, ssl) to learn normal behavior.
Add hunting pivots: use notice, files, and software logs to increase context around suspicious hosts.
Implement detections with scripts: subscribe to protocol events, create derived fields, and raise notices for patterns you care about.
Operationalize: ship logs to your platform, tune filters, and iterate based on false positives and gaps.
when: You need high quality network telemetry for investigations, not just alerts.
You want to write detections based on protocol behavior and metadata at scale.
You are building a SOC pipeline and want consistent logs that work well with search and analytics.
notes: Zeek is only as good as its visibility. SPAN misconfigurations, asymmetric routing, or missing VLANs can silently break analysis.
Start small. A handful of well understood logs beats turning on everything and drowning in noise.
Custom scripting is powerful, but performance and data volume matter. Treat scripts like production code and test changes.
Zeek generates logs by design. Detections come from how you query, enrich, and script that telemetry.
proTips: Learn conn.log deeply. It is the pivot point for most investigations and joins naturally to other logs.
Use the Notice framework to standardize alerts and keep your detection logic auditable.
commonMistakes: Assuming missing detections are a scripting problem when the real issue is sensor visibility or capture loss.
Turning on too many logs and frameworks on day one, then failing to build a usable baseline.
Not planning for rotation and ingestion, which leads to data loss or pipeline bottlenecks.

sections.title: Why Zeek feels different: telemetry, not signatures
paragraphs: Many tools try to answer “is this bad?” immediately. Zeek’s superpower is answering “what happened?” with high fidelity. It records structured facts about connections and protocols, which lets you search, correlate, and build detections that survive small attacker changes.

For example, conn.log captures who communicated, when, how long, and over which transport. Protocol logs then add meaning: dns.log shows name resolution behavior, http.log shows methods and URIs, and TLS logs show certificate and handshake metadata. This layered view is the foundation for both hunting and detection engineering.

sections.title: Logs as a language: how Zeek writes evidence
paragraphs: Zeek’s logging framework controls what gets written, how it is rotated, and how it can be post processed. Rotation is not just housekeeping. It shapes how your pipeline tails files, how you batch ingest data, and how you keep time aligned during investigations.

Core logs are intentionally stable. You can rely on them to build dashboards and saved searches. When you need more context, you extend logs by adding fields in scripts or by enabling additional analyzers and packages.

sections.title: Event driven scripting: turning protocol parsing into detections
paragraphs: Zeek’s scripting language is event driven. Protocol analyzers raise events as they parse traffic, and your scripts can react in near real time. This is how you build custom detections without writing a full parser yourself.

A useful mindset is “subscribe, enrich, decide”. Subscribe to an event that represents something meaningful, enrich it with local context or intelligence, then decide whether to log it, tag it, or raise a notice. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes scripts easier to tune and safer to operate.

sections.title: Frameworks: Notice, Intel, and File Analysis
paragraphs: Frameworks are reusable building blocks exposed to scripts. The Notice framework gives you a consistent way to emit alerts with the right fields and context. The Intel framework ingests indicators and matches them against observed traffic so enrichment is systematic rather than ad hoc.

The File Analysis framework is where Zeek becomes particularly useful for investigations. It can identify files transferred over supported protocols, compute hashes, extract metadata, and let you route high value artifacts into deeper analysis workflows.

sections.title: Operational reality: visibility, performance, and integration
paragraphs: Zeek can be deployed in many ways, but the operational constraints are always the same: you need reliable traffic visibility, predictable performance, and a log pipeline that will not drop data under load. If packets are missing, analyzers become less confident, and your logs can contain gaps or ambiguous results.

Treat Zeek as part of a system. Capture, parsing, rotation, shipping, and storage all have to work together. When you get that right, Zeek becomes a long term source of truth for network behavior that scales from day to day monitoring to incident response.

detectionTools.tagline: Network security monitor that turns packets into high fidelity, structured logs and events.
